transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janene Herbst.
Ukraine says it urgently needs more U.S. Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against incoming
Russian missiles.
But the paperwork to transfer those key weapons is stuck at the Pentagon, as NPR's Greg Mairi
reports.
A U.S. official confirmed to NPR that the authorization to send the Patriot missiles
to Ukraine is sitting on the desk of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon.
The official, who's not authorized to comment publicly on the issue, spoke to NPR's Tom
Bowman.
The story was first reported by The Washington Post.
The U.S. has stopped sending Patriots directly to Ukraine, but some NATO countries have been
willing to transfer small batches of 10 or so a month.
However, because these are U.S.-made weapons, the Pentagon must sign off before they can
be sent to Ukraine.
Russia can fire 20 or more missiles into Ukraine on a single night.
Greg Mairi, NPR News, Washington.
A Montana House race, now considered a toss-up, could be critical to hopes by Democrats to
control Congress.
As NPR's Sam Greenglass reports from Missoula, a former Forest Service smoke jumper is trying
to flip a seat by harnessing anger at corporate power and both parties.
Montana's first congressional district stretches some 400 miles from Yellowstone to Glacier
National Park.
Trump won it by double digits in 2024.
But 32-year-old populist Democrat Sam Forstag thinks he can win here by speaking from personal
experience about the economic stress facing many Montana voters.
"I was making 19 bucks an hour jumping out of airplanes for the federal government in
a community where you'd be lucky to find a home for less than a half million bucks.
If federal employees, like a smoke jumper, are being left behind, a whole lot of other
people are being left behind by both political parties."
If successful, the campaign could provide a playbook for Democrats to compete again
in territory they used to win but recently have struggled to hang on to.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Missoula.
Three-quarters of Albertans voted to remain in Canada in the oil-rich province's referendum
yesterday.
Reporter Sheena Rossiter has more from Alberta's capital, Edmonton.
Crowds cheer at the Forever Canadian campaign watch party hours after the polls closed.
They are part of the more than 76% of Albertans who voted to remain part of Canada.
Thomas Lukaszak is the founder of the Forever Canadian campaign and a former Conservative
deputy premier of Alberta.
If President Trump is watching this, he better be worried about his midterms because Canada
is not up for grabs.
Official results of this non-binding referendum are expected on October 29th.
For NPR News, I'm Sheena Rossiter in Edmonton.
While strating higher at this hour, the Dow is up 517 points, NASDAQ up 46.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Trump administration will soon roll out a first-of-its-kind federal voucher program
to help families pay for a range of education costs, including private school tuition.
As NPR's Corey Turner reports, states have to opt in or out of the program, and most
Democratic governors are still undecided.
Colorado's Jared Polis was the first and remains one of the only Democratic governors to opt
his state in to the new voucher program.
It's because he says it can also help public school families pay for things like tutoring
after school.
It could be for a summer program you otherwise couldn't afford, really great opportunities
for kids.
But Jessica Levin, with Education Law Center, sees the program as a Trojan horse.
The way to help public school, she says, is to fund them.
It is not to accept a privatization program that throws a few crumbs at public school
students.
16 undecided governors and the mayor of Washington, D.C. have until the end of the year to opt
in or out of the voucher program.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
A nor'easter is crawling up the east coast.
The National Weather Service says the storm, stationed well off the Carolinas, is expected
to intensify as it slowly heads north.
And while the rain is forecast to stay mostly offshore, gusty winds and coastal flooding
are still possible from the outer banks through New England in the next several days, and
rough surf and rip currents are expected.
Flood advisories have been issued up the Mid-Atlantic seaboard into New Jersey.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.
This week on Up First, the midterms less than 15 days away.
President Trump, Vice President J.D.
Vance and former President Obama all crisscrossing the country, rallying voters in key racist
from Michigan to Georgia to North Carolina.
Join us every morning as we guide you through the homestretch of this election season, Up
First, on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

topics.text: Ukraine urgently needs more U.S. Patriot missiles, but Pentagon authorization sits with Hegseth
Montana's first district House race becomes toss-up; Democrat Sam Forstag campaigns on economic stress
Over 76% of Albertans vote to remain in Canada in non-binding referendum
Trump administration rolls out federal education voucher program; most Democratic governors undecided
Nor'easter off the Carolinas brings coastal flood advisories and rough surf up the East Coast
Up First previews final stretch of midterm campaigns with Trump, Vance, and Obama rallying voters
